newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo elections expected to confirm Milosevic.
newsitem.headline: Yugo elections expected to confirm Milosevic.

text.p: Yugoslavia votes on Sunday in the country's first post-peace elections in which Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic is expected to consolidate his power by a comfortable victory over a coalition of opposition parties.

Polls put Milosevic's ruling Socialist Party (SPS) and two allied parties well ahead of the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition despite Yugoslavia's economic collapse under U.N. sanctions during the wars in Bosnia and Croatia.
Voters will elect a federal parliament and municipal authorities in Serbia and Montenegro, the two remaining Yugoslav republics.
A low-key election campaign ended on Thursday.
Milosevic, blamed by the West as the architect of former Yugoslavia's disintegration amid nationalist turmoil in 1991, is not a candidate in the elections.

But victory for the SPS and its allies -- the Marxist JUL headed by Milosevic's wife Mirjana and New Democracy (ND) -- will enable the Serbian leader to push through constitutional change that will allow him to stay in power when his second and last term as Serbian president expires in a year's time.
Political analysts expect him to take over as federal president after the next federal parliament invests the post, now mainly ceremonial, with strong executive authority.
Polls indicated the Socialist-led coalition would win around 50 per cent of the vote with Zajdano winning around 30 percent and the extreme nationalist Radical Party 10 percent.
The vote is the first in Yugoslavia since the Dayton peace agreement last year resulted in the ending of U.N. sanctions against Yugoslavia.
The easing of the country's international isolation has had little visible effect on living standards which plummeted during the war.
But Yugoslavia's impoverishment appears not to have damaged Milosevic's authority despite a recent increase in protests by workers demanding employment and the payment of unpaid wages.
He portrayed his Socialists during the campaign as guarantors of stability and future prosperity.
The opposition alliance suffered from a number of factors including lack of credibility and publicity after being ignored by the state-controlled media.

The coalition's slim chances of victory vanished early in the campaign when Dragoslav Avramovic, the respected former governor of the national bank who was fired by Milosevic last spring, stepped down as its leader.
Official results are not due before November 7 but the outcome was expected to be indicated early in the week by unofficial returns.
